taxonomyNote: NatureServe and SREL recognize two subspecies (C. c. coccinea and C. c. copei) and treat the Texas scarletsnake as a separate species, C. lineri.
fieldMarks: Slender, small to medium snake, 14-20 in (rarely to 32 in), with wide red bands bordered in black, separated by cream, white or light-yellow bands from head to tail.
Red, pointed snout and head; plain white or cream belly; smooth glossy scales.

Black bands separate the red bands from the yellow ones, which tells it from a coral snake; the plain white or cream belly separates it from scarlet kingsnakes and milksnakes, whose pattern extends onto the belly.
behavior: Nocturnal and secretive; spends most time underground or under cover and is seen mostly crossing roads on warm summer nights, especially after rain; surface activity mostly May-September, peaking June-July.
Eats mainly reptile eggs, pierced with enlarged rear teeth, plus small lizards, snakes, frogs and mice.
Lays 2-9 elongated white eggs underground in summer.
habitat: Pine or hardwood forest and woodland and adjacent open areas with sandy or loamy well-drained soil; also fields, grassy edges and roadsides near woods; found under logs, rocks, leaf litter or boards.
range: NatureServe lists it in the southeastern and south-central US, from New Jersey and Indiana south to Florida and west to Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas; Texas populations in SREL's account are a separate species (C. lineri). Not recorded for Canada.

lookalikes.name: Scarlet kingsnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Its bands encircle the whole body including the belly; scarlet snake has a plain white belly.

lookalikes.name: Eastern coral snake
lookalikes.howToTell: North Carolina WRC: scarlet snakes have black bands separating the wide red bands from the yellow bands, unlike coral snakes.
